st.headline: CNMC Goldmine shares plunge as gold falls below US$4,000
st.teaser: Spot gold fell 0.24% to US$3,872 an ounce on Nov 16.
fullText: SINGAPORE - Shares of CNMC Goldmine Holdings plunged on Nov 16, extending recent losses as gold prices dipped below US$4,000 an ounce following a sell-off in the precious metal.

The mainboard-listed mining stock sank nearly 11% to 85 cents at the midday trading break on Nov 16, bringing its losses to about 20.56% over the past five trading sessions and almost 30% over the past month.
About 5.5 million shares changed hands during the morning trading session on Nov 16.

Spot gold, meanwhile, fell 0.24% to US$3,872 (S$4,990) an ounce, as signs that the US Federal Reserve could raise rates weighed on sentiment. This came ahead of remarks by Fed chair Kevin Warsh at a Nov 16 US conference that could offer further clues on the direction of interest rates.
Gold has fallen nearly 6% since the start of the year, as elevated US Treasury yields and a stronger greenback dampened demand for the precious metal.
CNMC’s net profit rose 17.8% to US$18.6 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026, from US$15.8 million a year earlier.

The Singapore-headquartered gold and base metals producer, which operates in Kelantan, Malaysia, generated US$65.2 million in revenue for first half of 2026, up 23.4% from a year earlier, driven by higher gold, silver and zinc prices.
Revenue from gold produced at its carbon-in-leach plant at its flagship Sokor mine increased 32% to US$49.8 million.
Revenue from gold produced at its flagship Sokor mine’s carbon-in-leach plant rose 32% to US$49.8 million, even as production fell 6% to 11,105 ounces.

Including gold produced from lead concentrate at its flotation plant, which is used primarily to recover base metals, the company generated total revenue of US$56.7 million from gold in the first half of 2026, a 27.4% increase from a year earlier.
Still, CNMC’s all-in production cost is about US$2000 per ounce, so margins would still be intact even if gold retreats further.

cna.headline: India's Mphasis says clients boost cybersecurity spending as AI-driven threats rise
cna.teaser: India's Mphasis says clients boost cybersecurity spending as AI-driven threats rise
fullText: Nov 16 : Blackstone-backed Mphasis said companies globally are increasing cybersecurity spending in the race to strengthen their defences, CEO Nitin Rakesh told Reuters, as AI enables increasingly sophisticated attacks that are faster and cheaper.

Banks and insurers are leading the increase in cybersecurity spending, aided by larger technology budgets and regulatory requirements, while retailers and consumer firms are also stepping up investments to protect customer data, Rakesh said last week, without providing figures.

The comments follow a record $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance last month, in which hackers used social engineering and compromised AI tools, highlighting the growing complexity of cyber threats.
Against that backdrop, companies are stepping up cybersecurity spending as AI makes attacks faster and cheaper and increases the number of vulnerabilities they must address.
A related survey found awareness of advanced AI cyber threats prompted 85 per cent of organisations to plan higher security spending, versus 64 per cent after suffering a breach.
Rakesh said clients were increasingly investing in identity and access controls covering employees, software accounts and automated agents, while also using AI to detect and fix vulnerabilities.
While threat detection is already heavily automated, fixing vulnerabilities still requires significant manual work, he said.
"You can't really throw people at that problem because you won't be able to keep up with the volume that is required in the time-frame that you need to fix those patches," Rakesh said.

economistArticle.title: The Counter-Weight Market: India's Hedge Against Tech Turbulence
paras: For the past two years, global equity indices have danced to a single tune: the dizzying ascent of artificial intelligence and its hardware enablers. Semiconductor giants in Taiwan, South Korea, and the United States have captured the lion's share of foreign portfolio inflows, driving valuations to lofty heights. Yet this intense concentration has left fund managers vulnerable to any sudden correction in tech sentiment.

Intriguingly, an inverse relationship has begun to emerge between global tech hardware stocks and South Asian equities. When enthusiasm for semiconductor manufacturers falters, global investors often pivot towards market segments that rely less on silicon cycles and more on domestic consumption. India, with its vast internal market and consumer-driven economy, has increasingly functioned as an anti-AI trade.

This negative correlation stems from fundamental differences in economic architecture. Unlike East Asian export powerhouses whose fortunes are tethered to global technology spending, India's corporate earnings depend heavily on domestic credit growth, infrastructure spending, and financial services. Consequently, broad pullbacks in global technology stocks spark capital reallocation rather than widespread capitulation.

Moreover, high semiconductor valuations have prompted institutional investors to seek valuation shelter. While chipmakers trade at demanding multiples premised on perpetual growth, Indian financial and industrial firms offer earnings visibility grounded in tangible domestic demand. The flow of funds acts as an automatic stabilizer for emerging market portfolios seeking shelter from hardware volatility.

Whether this inverse dynamic endures depends on how global macroeconomic conditions evolve. If artificial intelligence hype cools permanently, foreign capital may permanently recalibrate its emerging market weightings. In an era marked by technological unpredictability, India’s insulation from the silicon cycle presents a compelling counterweight for risk-conscious investors.
economistArticle.cn:
在过去两年中，全球股票指数一直围绕着同一个主题起舞：人工智能及其硬件支持者的令人眩目的崛起。台湾、韩国和美国的半导体巨头吸纳了大部分外资证券投资，将估值推向高位。然而，这种高度集中也使基金经理更容易受到科技股情绪突然回调的影响。

有趣的是，全球科技硬件股票与南亚股市之间开始呈现出一种逆向关系。当市场对半导体制造商的热情衰退时，全球投资者往往会转向那些较少依赖芯片周期、更多依赖内需的市场板块。凭借庞大的国内市场和消费驱动型经济，印度越来越扮演起“反人工智能交易”的角色。

这种负相关性源于经济结构的根本差异。与财富紧密挂钩于全球科技支出的东亚出口强国不同，印度的企业盈利高度依赖于国内信贷增长、基础设施投资和金融服务。因此，全球科技股的广泛回调引发的是资本重新配置，而非泛的抛售投降。

此外，半导体板块的高估值促使机构投资者寻找估值避风港。虽然芯片制造商的交易估值处于以永久增长为前提的高倍数水平，但印度的金融和工业企业却提供了依托于实体内需的清晰盈利可见度。资金流动充当了新兴市场投资组合抵御硬件波动影响的自动稳定器。

这种逆向动态能否持续，取决于全球宏观经济条件如何演变。如果人工智能的热潮永久降温，外资可能会永久重新调整其新兴市场的配置权重。在一个以技术不可预测性为特征的时代，印度对芯片周期的隔离效应为注重风险控制的投资者提供了一个强有力的平衡杠杆。
